questions.prompt: Why can equal amounts of adsorbed protein produce different cell responses on two materials?
options: Adsorbed proteins can differ in conformation, orientation, or accessible binding sites
Cells only sense bulk density
Protein amount fixes protein activity
Surface chemistry cannot affect cells

feedback.hint: Quantity is not the same as biological presentation.
feedback.solution: Surface chemistry can alter protein conformation, orientation, and epitope accessibility even when total adsorbed mass is similar.

questions.prompt: A scaffold loses 15% of its remaining mass each week under a simplified first-order model. If initial mass is 100 mg and the same fraction is lost each week, what mass remains after one week?

feedback.hint: Multiply the initial mass by the fraction retained, 1−0.15.
feedback.solution: 100 mg×0.85=85 mg. Repeated weekly fractional loss would compound as 100×0.85ⁿ.

modifications: Replaced 'initial mass' with 'remaining mass' to make constant fractional loss agree with the stated first-order model.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly supports functional cartilage regeneration?
options: A single chondrogenic transcript is elevated
The construct bears relevant load, forms appropriate matrix, and integrates with host tissue
The scaffold has a blue dye
More cells were seeded initially

feedback.hint: Look for a functional outcome aligned with the target tissue.
feedback.solution: Functionally relevant mechanical performance, tissue composition, and integration collectively support regeneration more strongly than one marker alone.

questions.prompt: What is the best definition of biocompatibility?
options: No immune cell ever contacts the material
Appropriate material performance with a host response suited to the application
The material never degrades
The same response in every tissue

feedback.hint: Biological response is judged in the context of a specific use.
feedback.solution: Biocompatibility is application-specific: a material must perform with an appropriate host response for its intended purpose.

questions.prompt: Two polymer films have the same bulk composition and modulus. One was plasma-treated to make its surface more hydrophilic. Protein adsorption and cell attachment differ between them. Which interpretation is best?
options: Surface chemistry and energy can change the biological response without changing bulk properties, so both must be characterized.
The difference must come from a bulk stiffness change.
Identical bulk composition guarantees identical cell response.
Surface treatments cannot alter protein adsorption.

feedback.hint: Separate what the cell touches from what the sample is made of.
feedback.solution: Cells and proteins contact the surface, so wettability, charge, chemistry and topography can change adsorption and attachment while bulk composition and modulus stay the same. A design brief therefore needs surface and bulk measurements.

questions.prompt: A degradable scaffold's modulus is modeled as E(t) = E0·exp(−k t) with E0 = 2.0 MPa and k = 0.05 day⁻¹. Calculate E at t = 14 days. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Compute k·t first.
feedback.solution: k·t = 0.70 and E = 2.0 × e^−0.70 = 0.993 MPa. This is a first-order model of one property; real degradation changes mass, porosity and modulus at different rates.

questions.prompt: A design brief aims to form cartilage-like matrix in vitro. Which plan best maps components to the goal?
options: A scaffold chosen only for how easily it is manufactured.

A chondrogenic cell source, a hydrated scaffold with stiffness in a relevant range, biochemical cues that support matrix production, and loading conditions chosen for the goal, each with a measurable readout.
Any scaffold, because cells determine the outcome regardless of mechanics.
A stiff mineralized scaffold with no biochemical cues.

feedback.hint: Match cells, scaffold, cues and mechanics to one stated goal.
feedback.solution: Tissue-engineering design links four elements to a stated goal: a suitable cell source, a scaffold with appropriate properties, biochemical cues and mechanical conditions, and each needs a readout. This is an in-vitro design exercise and says nothing about clinical performance.

questions.prompt: In a case study, a synthetic implant material attracts a thick fibrous capsule that isolates it from surrounding tissue and degrades its intended function. Which failure-mode category does this illustrate?
options: A sterilization step that was skipped.
A manufacturing tolerance error only.
A host (foreign-body) response, which is different from mechanical fatigue or toxic degradation products.
Mechanical fatigue of the bulk material.

feedback.hint: Classify by cause: host response, mechanics, chemistry or process.
feedback.solution: Encapsulation is a host response to the material. Case studies separate failure modes by cause (host response, mechanical failure, degradation chemistry, process error), because each calls for a different investigation.

questions.prompt: A hydrogel loses mass by first-order kinetics with k = 0.05 per day. Calculate its half-life and enter it as a value with a time unit in hours (for example 100 h).

feedback.hint: t½ = ln 2 / k; then convert days to hours.

questions.prompt: With first-order degradation at k = 0.05 per day, what percentage of the initial mass remains after 30 days? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Remaining fraction is e^(−kt).

questions.prompt: A protein with diffusion coefficient 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s in a gel must leave a slab of half-thickness 1 mm. Estimate the characteristic release time τ = L²/D. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use L in meters, then convert seconds to hours.

questions.prompt: For the same protein (D = 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s), the slab half-thickness is reduced to 0.5 mm. Estimate the new release time. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Release time scales with the square of the distance.
feedback.solution: τ = (5.0×10⁻⁴)² / 10⁻¹⁰ = 2500 s = 0.69 h, a quarter of the 1 mm value.

questions.prompt: A growth factor diffuses out of a gel in about 3 hours, while the gel's degradation half-life is about 14 days and the target repair process takes weeks. Which change most directly aligns release with the repair timeline?
options: Use a thinner gel.
Make the gel degrade faster.
Tether or affinity-bind the growth factor to the network so it is freed as the gel degrades.
Load more growth factor so the burst is larger.

feedback.hint: Which time scale do you want release to follow?
feedback.solution: Release is diffusion-controlled and far faster than degradation. Binding the cargo to the network ties release to degradation. Faster degradation, a bigger burst or a thinner gel would all shorten or front-load the release.

questions.prompt: A degradable implant keeps its dimensions for weeks while its mass and strength fall steadily, then fragments. Which erosion mode does this describe, and what condition favors it?
options: Surface erosion, favored by hydrophilic materials.
Surface erosion, favored when bond cleavage is faster than water penetration.
Bulk erosion, favored when water penetrates the material faster than bonds are cleaved.
No erosion; the strength loss is due to cell infiltration only.

feedback.hint: Compare the speed of water entry with the speed of bond breaking.
feedback.solution: When water reaches the interior before bonds break, degradation is distributed through the volume: shape is retained while mass and strength fall, and late fragmentation is possible. Surface erosion shrinks the device from outside in.

questions.prompt: A scaffold has an apparent density equal to 10% of the density of its solid polymer. Calculate its porosity as a percentage. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Porosity is one minus relative density.

questions.prompt: An open-cell scaffold has relative density 0.1 and is made from a solid with modulus 1000 MPa. Using E*/E_s ≈ (ρ*/ρ_s)², estimate the scaffold modulus. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Square the relative density and multiply by the solid modulus.

questions.prompt: The same material is made at relative density 0.2 instead of 0.1. Estimate the new modulus with the same scaling. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Doubling relative density multiplies a square law by four.
feedback.solution: E* ≈ 1000 × 0.2² = 40 MPa, four times the 10 MPa value.

questions.prompt: Medium (μ = 10⁻³ Pa·s) flows through a scaffold of permeability 10⁻¹⁰ m², cross-section 1 cm² and thickness 5 mm under a pressure drop of 10 Pa. Using Q = k A ΔP / (μ L), calculate the flow rate. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Work in SI units (m², m, Pa, Pa·s) to get m³/s, then convert.

questions.prompt: A team lowers scaffold porosity from 90% to 80% to stop collapse during culture. Which combination of effects should they expect for an open-cell scaffold?
options: Stiffness doubles and permeability is unchanged.
Stiffness roughly quadruples, while void volume falls and permeability typically drops, which can slow nutrient transport and cell infiltration.
Permeability rises because there is more surface area.
Stiffness is unchanged because the material is the same.

feedback.hint: Apply the square law to relative density 0.1 → 0.2, then think about pores.
feedback.solution: Relative density doubles, so the square law quadruples the modulus. Less void and usually smaller or fewer pores lower permeability. The fix for collapse costs transport, which is the central scaffold trade-off.

questions.prompt: A paper states that a scaffold 'matches the stiffness of cartilage' based on one compressive modulus measured on dry samples at a single strain rate. What is the main weakness of this claim?
options: Compression tests cannot measure modulus.
Tissue and hydrated scaffold mechanics are nonlinear, anisotropic and rate-dependent, so a single dry modulus does not establish a match under physiological conditions.
Cartilage has no measurable stiffness.
There is no weakness if the numbers agree.

feedback.hint: Ask how, under what conditions and against what reference the comparison was made.
feedback.solution: Hydration, test mode, strain rate and direction can change measured moduli substantially. A credible match compares like-for-like tests under physiological conditions, and cells sense local rather than bulk stiffness.
